title: Defcon's new badge is a security key you can see inside
gist: This year's Defcon badge is built around the Baochip-1x, a mostly open source RISC-V microcontroller from hardware hacker Andrew 'bunnie' Huang whose package lets infrared light through the silicon so researchers can visually verify the manufactured chip matches the published design. The 27,000 badges are the chip's first mass distribution, and the detachable module works after the conference as a FIDO security token intended as a more inspectable alternative to existing hardware keys and crypto wallets.

insights.claim: The Baochip-1x is packaged so infrared light can be shone through the back of the silicon, letting researchers visually inspect internal structures such as RAM arrays and compare them against the published design instead of trusting the fab.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Optical verifiability turns hardware trust from a paper audit into a physical check — a template competitors in secure silicon will be pressured to match.
insights.locator: Unlike conventional chips encased in opaque plastic

insights.claim: Earlier open source chips still shipped in impermeable plastic packaging, leaving a supply-chain gap where a backdoor could be inserted at manufacturing without users being able to detect it.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Open specs alone never closed the fab-level trust gap; this reframes where hardware-security spending has to go.
insights.locator: Computer chips are traditionally black-box components

insights.claim: Huang has published source code for the Baochip's operating system, firmware, processor core, cryptographic engines and input-output system on GitHub, after three years of development.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A full-stack open security microcontroller lowers the barrier for anyone building auditable authentication or wallet hardware.

insights.claim: Some low-level physical-design and manufacturing elements tied to TSMC's 22-nanometer process remain proprietary, so the Baochip is 'mostly' rather than fully open source.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Foundry-owned physical IP is the hard limit on chip openness — no design effort removes that dependency.
insights.locator: There are some closed-source elements on Huang's chip

insights.claim: Huang funded the chip by piggybacking his CPU onto Crossbar's wafer so both designs shared one manufacturing run, avoiding the millions of dollars a dedicated fabrication run would have cost.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Wafer-sharing is a repeatable route for small teams to get custom silicon made — a structurally cheaper path than the headline mask-set cost implies.
insights.quote: They look at it as, if they put me on the chip, they get two products for the price of one,

insights.claim: Huang says this kind of piggybacking on another company's manufacturing run is not unusual in the semiconductor industry, though it is not something the industry likes to discuss publicly.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Undisclosed shared wafer runs mean the same die can carry multiple parties' logic — a due-diligence question for anyone auditing chip provenance.

insights.claim: The Crossbar and Baochip parts are physically the same chip with different CPU cores activated: Crossbar's version enables a proprietary ARM core, while Huang's enables an open source RISC-V core and disables Crossbar's processor.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shared infrastructure with swappable cores shows how RISC-V gets into production silicon by riding ARM-based programs rather than displacing them outright.
insights.locator: The Crossbar version of the chip uses a proprietary ARM core

insights.claim: The 27,000 Defcon badges are the Baochip's first major distribution, after the chip had only been available in a small development release.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Seeding tens of thousands of units into the hands of security researchers is a cheap adoption bootstrap that no marketing budget replicates.

insights.claim: Defcon founder Jeff Moss required that the badge have a life beyond the conference rather than ending up in a drawer or landfill, which is why the badge's core module detaches and works as a standalone token.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Designing conference hardware for post-event utility is how a one-off giveaway becomes an installed base.
insights.locator: Moss had one requirement for the badges

insights.claim: Moss backed the project because he has long been frustrated that existing hardware security tokens and crypto wallets can be cracked at the hardware level, and saw Huang's chip as a more secure alternative.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Hardware-level extraction risk in wallets and keys is the addressable weakness the Baochip is aimed at — relevant to every self-custody hardware vendor.
insights.locator: He's long been frustrated with the design and limitations

insights.claim: The detachable badge module works as a FIDO hardware security token with support for time-based one-time passwords and password management, plus a camera for scanning QR codes to register authentication systems.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: It ships as a functional YubiKey substitute on day one, not a dev board — that is what makes the adoption push credible.
insights.quote: probably the world’s first open source security token that you can fully inspect all the way down to the bootloader [and] transistors.
insights.locator: The badge's detachable module can serve as a FIDO hardware security token

insights.claim: The badge camera is deliberately low resolution and nearsighted, uses only black-and-white data by default and cannot store photos, to comply with Defcon's ban on surreptitious photography.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Capability-limited sensors are a design pattern for shipping useful hardware into privacy-hostile environments.
insights.quote: It’s … great at scanning QR codes and pretty much bad at everything else,
insights.locator: The removable module also includes a camera

insights.claim: The Baochip runs a Rust-based operating system with secure boot, a true random number generator and hardening features, and Huang expects it to be particularly resistant to remote, nonphysical attacks.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: The claimed strength is remote attack resistance, which is the threat model that matters for authentication tokens in practice.

insights.claim: The chip stores data in resistive RAM rather than flash, because de-layered flash cells expose stored ones and zeros directly to visual inspection while RRAM makes physical extraction harder.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Memory technology choice, not just crypto, determines whether a device survives physical teardown — a differentiator for secure-element vendors.
insights.locator: The chip also uses resistive RAM

insights.claim: Huang estimates the chip could withstand attacks costing tens of thousands of dollars but would likely fall to an adversary with millions of dollars and a sophisticated hardware-analysis lab.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: An explicit dollar-denominated threat ceiling is rare in security hardware marketing and gives buyers a real basis for comparison.
insights.quote: I actually think it’s one of the most secure chips you can get out there, but I [also] think most chips have been oversold in terms of security,
insights.locator: Huang is cautious, however, about overhyping

insights.claim: Huang treats the Defcon launch as an intentional stress test and expects attendees to find zero-days in the open code, framing discovered flaws as a feature of launching there.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Crowd-sourced adversarial testing at scale is a faster hardening path than private audits, and a reason to watch post-conference disclosures.
insights.quote: I fully expect there will be zero-days [that people find in the code].
insights.locator: Huang says he likes the fact that the chip will be stress-tested

insights.claim: The Baochip uses a 350 MHz RISC-V processor with 2 MB of SRAM, 4 MB of RRAM and four 700 MHz PicoRV32 I/O cores, already runs MicroPython with C and Rust development kits, and sits on the edge of being able to run Linux.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Those specs put it beyond token duty and into HSM or general-purpose secure-compute territory, widening the addressable use cases.
insights.quote: on the edge of being able to run Linux
insights.locator: Today the chip can function as a YubiKey-like security token
